To my knowledge, there isn't a specific convention for template type naming for templates with multiple types. T and S are valid choices, but it would improve readability to name the template types after the specific data members whose types they represent. For example, there is no indication that `T` represents `batteryLife`'s type, but `TBatteryLife` or some equivalent would make it clear.

This is not the proper way to implement a constructor in C++. You should instead use a member initializer list, which takes the following form in this case:
```c++
SmartWatch(T b, S v, string m) : batteryLife(b), version(v), model(m) {}
```
When you do not use a member initializer list, rather than directly constructing the data member with the given initial value, it instead *default constructs* each data member, then reassigns their value to the given initial value. This is a very important thing to keep in mind when programming C++.

We still need the private data members batteryLife and version, but once you declare the templated types in line 10:
template <typename T1, typename T2>

batteryLife can be type T1 and version can be type T2. Thus, lines 8 and 9 will be
T1 batteryLife;
T2 version;

Then pass the corresponding parameters into the SmartWatch constructor:
SmartWatch(T1 b, T2 v, string m).

Basically replace all types of batteryLife with T1 and version with T2 instead of hardcoding their types. This way, you don't have to modify the input values to match specific types below.

use template <typename T1, typename T2>, this way the method is able to accept multiple types as the parameters. This allows you to reuse the same method for multiple different types and don't need to rewrite another method for handling other types. High level way to think of it is battery and version can be both ints and doubles, etc. hope this helps!
